content: Recovery, Inc. employs a method that is fundamentally rooted in cognitive therapy. This approach assists individuals in recognizing potential errors or misconceptions in their perception of reality. Because the methods used by Recovery, Inc. do not conflict with other therapeutic approaches, they can be effectively integrated with twelve-step programs. Mental health professionals frequently recommend this method as a supplementary tool to enhance ongoing therapy. Participants are encouraged to identify physical sensations or racing thoughts and to spot the thoughts that preceded these experiences. Other group members provide alternative perspectives on the situation and suggest strategies for managing similar symptoms in the future. For instance, an individual might experience depression, referred to as lowered feelings in Recovery terminology, due to striving for perfection. The pursuit of perfection or the desire to appear flawless can lead to feelings of despair when even minor mistakes occur. Members are taught to endorse themselves, meaning they give themselves credit for their efforts rather than solely for their successes. All improvements, no matter how small, are acknowledged. Members are instructed to compare themselves only to their past selves, rather than to others. Longstanding members are encouraged to share their successes with the Recovery methods to support newcomers. Former mental health patients who participated in Recovery, Inc. reported no greater anxiety about their mental health than the general population. Members rated their life satisfaction levels as high or even higher than those of the general public. Those who had participated for two years or more reported the highest levels of satisfaction with their health. Conversely, members with less than two years of participation were more likely to still be taking medication, living below the poverty line, and having smaller social networks. Participation in Recovery, Inc. was associated with a reduction in symptoms of mental illness and a decreased need for psychiatric treatment. Approximately half of the members had been hospitalized prior to joining the program. After joining, less than 8% of members experienced hospitalization. Scores of neurotic distress among members decreased, and longstanding members demonstrated psychological well-being scores comparable to those of a control group in the same community. Long-term members required less psychiatric medication and psychotherapy compared to newer members.
